mainEntity.name: How do you answer why do you want to work here?

acceptedAnswer.text: Connect a verified detail about the company or team to work you want to do, then explain why that work fits your experience or interests. Keep the answer specific enough that you could not give it unchanged to every employer.

mainEntity.name: What if I do not know much about the company?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the job description, the company's own product or service pages, and any relevant team materials. Choose one useful detail you can verify. Ask about what remains unclear instead of inventing enthusiasm or claiming insider knowledge.

mainEntity.name: Can I mention pay or remote work as a reason for applying?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, those can be legitimate reasons. You can discuss practical fit directly while also explaining which responsibilities interest you and what you would contribute. You do not need to pretend that compensation or working arrangements are irrelevant.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between why this company and why this role?

acceptedAnswer.text: Why this company focuses on the organization, its work, or the team you would join. Why this role focuses on the responsibilities. A useful answer connects both rather than describing the company's reputation alone.

h1: Why Do You Want to Work Here? Research and Answer Examples
lead: Answer why do you want to work here with specific company research, an honest reason for your interest, and examples for graduates and career changers.
author: Amigo Team

hero.alt: A professional researching a potential employer at a laptop beside an office window.

html:
A strong answer to “Why do you want to work here?” connects something specific about the employer to work you actually want to do. Explain what caught your attention, why it matters to you, and how your experience fits. You do not need a lifelong attachment to the brand.

Maybe you found the opening yesterday. Maybe a recruiter contacted you. Maybe the company makes software you have never used. You can still give an honest, thoughtful answer. The preparation is to learn enough to explain why this opportunity deserves a closer look.

Microsoft's interview guidance asks candidates to research beyond the position itself, including the company and industry. That supports the basic approach here; the research checklist and examples below are our own suggestions.

What should you research before answering?

Begin with the job description. Circle the responsibilities you would spend time on, not just the desirable qualifications. A role that mentions customer implementations repeatedly may be quite different from one focused on long-term product development, even if both carry the same title.

Then read the employer's description of its product or service. Who uses it? What problem does it address? Find one detail connected to the role. If you are interviewing for an engineering position, a relevant engineering article may be useful. For operations, look for the actual service or workflow the company delivers.

Keep three short notes:

  • Verified detail: What did the employer actually say, and where?
  • Your connection: What interests you about that work?
  • Open question: What would you still need to understand before accepting?

Separate facts from assumptions. A company announcing a new product does not establish that your team will work on it. You can say it prompted your interest and ask whether it connects to the role.

A simple answer structure

Try this sequence: specific work → personal connection → contribution.

“The role's focus on [specific work] caught my attention. I enjoyed [relevant experience] because [honest reason]. I would like to apply that experience to [responsibility], and I am interested in learning more about [team question].”

This is a planning aid. Remove the brackets and rewrite it in your own voice. You do not have to make every answer the same length or end it with a question. As a rehearsal target, keep the opening answer around a minute and leave room for discussion.

Example: An experienced candidate

All examples in this article are fictional. The employer details are placeholders, not statements about a named company's hiring plans.

“The part of the job description that stood out was improving the tools your support team uses. In my current role, I have enjoyed working directly with support to understand where internal tools slow them down. I like being able to see the effect of a small product change on someone's daily work. This position seems to combine that kind of collaboration with more ownership of the technical design, which is a direction I want to grow in.”

The candidate explains the attraction without flattering the company. If the interviewer clarifies that the job has little direct contact with support, that is useful information about fit.

Example: A graduate

“I was interested in the way this analyst role combines investigating data with explaining the findings to operations teams. In my course project, I enjoyed working out why the numbers differed between two reports and presenting the explanation to people who had not done the analysis. I would like a role where those communication skills matter alongside the technical work. I also wanted to ask how new analysts learn the business context here.”

You do not need to manufacture a personal connection to the product. A real interest in the work is enough to explain, provided you have checked that the role includes it.

Example: A career changer

“I am moving from teaching into learning design, and this role's focus on practical training caught my attention. I have spent several years adapting explanations when learners get stuck, and I want to apply that experience to materials people use at work. Your description of building training with subject experts is particularly relevant. I would be bringing experience with learning needs while developing the production skills specific to this role.”

The answer makes the transition understandable and names a skill still being developed. For the broader career story, pair it with our “tell me about yourself” framework.

What if your main reasons are practical?

Pay, location, stability, and flexibility affect whether a job works for you. You do not need to deny that. You also need enough information about the responsibilities to explain why you want to do this particular job.

For example: “The working arrangement is a good fit for me, and the role also includes the customer onboarding work I want to keep developing. I would like to understand how the team divides its time between new implementations and ongoing support.”

That is more honest than claiming a deep passion for a company you have just discovered. Keep practical questions clear rather than burying them in an exaggerated statement of enthusiasm.

Check your answer before the interview

Replace the company name with another employer's. If the answer still works without any other changes, add a relevant detail. “Innovative company with a great culture” is a claim; a responsibility you want to take on gives the listener something concrete.

Check the detail against the source again. If an article describes a project from several years ago, say what interested you about it and ask whether that work is still relevant. Do not present an old announcement as a current team priority.

Finally, practice without reading. Keep the facts accurate, but let the wording vary. If the conversation changes your understanding of the role, update your answer. You are allowed to become more interested, less interested, or interested for a different reason after you learn more.

Our “why should we hire you” guide covers the related question about what you would contribute. Keep the two answers connected without giving the same speech twice.
